b: Is detox an accurate term to apply specifically to technology use? In addition to, or as an alternative to detox, what about using and applying the concept of choice?

Questions worth considering: Why would the term we choose to apply matter? Would it make any difference? One way to consider these questions is to recognize that choice is central to how human beings understand conscious action, voluntary behavior, the self, and agency (Liljenström, 2022; Shepherd, 2012).

Some may argue that technology use may become “habitual.” However, a “habit” may imply a lack of consciousness, free will, intention, or the ability to make decisions. Human beings possess all of these capacities. As such, a habit remains a choice. It is undertaken by a conscious individual capable of deciding what to think, do, say, learn, and choose (Liljenström, 2022; Purje, 2014; Shepherd, 2012).
To claim, “I cannot help myself because it is a habit,” is to shift responsibility from the self to a description of behavior. Behavior is a self-directed conscious choice (Roskies, 2006).
Habits Do Not Choose, People Choose
A habit may become familiar, but familiarity does not extinguish free will. Responsibility and accountability cannot be delegated to a habit (Wood & Rünger, 2016).

The language of detox may imply that "habitual" technology use is something done to us rather than something we actively choose and regulate. The most powerful example of this is found in the words of Viktor Frankl, who lived in the most abhorrent circumstances imaginable (Bushkin et al., 2021).

In a physical location over which he possessed virtually no control or power, Frankl, amazingly and profoundly, gained the insight that is often encapsulated in the following observation: “Between stimulus and response there is a space. In that space is our power to choose our response. In our response lies our growth and our freedom.”
How this insight and these words were even possible is beyond my comprehension. And yet they are there.

More remarkable still is the fact that this declaration did not emerge from comfort, security, privilege, or academic abstraction. It emerged, as noted, from circumstances that extinguished individuality, dignity, freedom, and any level of hope.
Yet—unbelievably—Frankl was, somehow, able to gain the insight to identify—a freedom—that could not be controlled or destroyed: the freedom to choose one's attitude and response.

In doing so, Frankl, for me, consciously, and in immutable terms, illuminated what could perhaps be one of the most profound insights ever articulated about consciousness, the universal human condition, and free will; while circumstances can constrain what happens to us, they do not control our attitude and choices (Frankl, 1946/2006).

Therefore, in terms of freedom, computer and technology use is a choice. This indicates we are responsible and accountable for our choices, and, in doing so, we also need to recognize that choices always lead to consequences and to stop blaming others for the choices we make (Wood & Rünger, 2016).

Consequently, regarding choices, consider the following: When a digital device is placed in front of an infant for hours each day, the child will tend to spend less time moving, exploring their external world, babbling, looking, listening, and interacting with their surroundings, and—most important of all—less time looking at and listening to their family. This will potentially have a significant impact on the child's brain (Massaroni et al., 2024; Nimmo & Chau, 2026).
This Is Not a Trivial Matter

During the developmental period when the brain is shaped by movement, curiosity, language, play, and human interaction, the choice of repeatedly replacing these experiences with a digital device is potentially catastrophic (Tierney & Nelson, 2009).

Every hour spent passively engaged with a screen is an hour not spent participating in the activities where the all-important neurological, cognitive, neuromuscular, social, linguistic, and cultural family nuance development occurs (Tierney & Nelson, 2009).

Choice and consequences are inseparable. So, where to from here? There are choices to be made, for which you are responsible and accountable. This includes the development of the child, as well as the use of computers (Frazier et al., 2021; Purje, 2014).

What this means is that choice extends beyond individual behavior to also that of collectives, from the small to the mighty and powerful. Consequently, this intrinsic capacity also becomes, as Immanuel Kant noted, an ethical and moral obligation, not only for the individual but also for the collective.
This ethical and moral obligation and principle holds that human beings must always be treated as ends in themselves and never merely as means to an end.

Viktor Frankl's observations further reinforce this principle: “Between stimulus and response there is space.” It is in this space that choices are made. Because of free will, these choices can be ethical and moral or unethical and immoral. Each choice will have a consequence (Bushkin et al., 2021; Lavazza, 2016; Shepherd, 2015).

Regarding technological development, media reports and a government declaration indicate that governments have recognized that social media corporations have an ethical and moral responsibility to ensure their products do not potentially harm users (Australian Government, 2024).

This insight aligns with the categorical imperative of Immanuel Kant; Kant argues that everyone must always be treated as an end in themselves and never merely as a means to an end. As such, choice, responsibility, accountability, and consequences extend beyond the individual to the collective.
Ethical Responsibility in the Age of Technology

Therefore, what is presented to the public through technology needs to be ethical and moral. For this reason, it is essential that as technological products are developed, all collectives consider their potential impact on a user's brain, mind, thinking, emotions, and behavior.

This universal social truth also emphasizes the enduring social and collective importance of ethical responsibility, moral accountability, principled choices, and constructive consequences (Burr et al., 2020; Grosman-Rimon & Wegier, 2024; Meier et al., 2025).
